## Introduction

The **Cauchy distribution** is a continuous probability distribution
notable for its heavy tails: it has no finite mean or variance. It arises
as the ratio of two independent standard normal random variables and as
the [[students-t-distribution]] with one degree of freedom.

:::{.definition data-title="Cauchy Distribution"}

A random variable $X$ follows a **Cauchy distribution** with location
parameter $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ and scale parameter $\gamma > 0$ if

$$
X \sim \text{Cauchy}(x_0, \gamma).
$$

:::

The **standard Cauchy distribution** is the case $x_0 = 0$, $\gamma = 1$.

## Probability Density Function

:::{.definition data-title="Probability Density Function (PDF)"}

The probability density function is

$$
f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi\gamma
  \left[1 + \left(\dfrac{x - x_0}{\gamma}\right)^2\right]},
  \quad x \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

:::

*Interpretation:* The density is symmetric and bell-shaped about $x_0$,
but its tails decay only like $x^{-2}$, so extreme values occur far more
often than for the [[normal-distribution]].

::: {#4b3f8327 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Plotting code"}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy.stats import cauchy, norm

sns.set_style('whitegrid')
sns.set_palette('Set2')

x = np.linspace(-6, 6, 500)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(x, cauchy.pdf(x), lw=2, label='Cauchy(0, 1)')
ax.plot(x, norm.pdf(x), lw=2, ls='--',
        label=r'$\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$')

ax.set_xlabel('$x$')
ax.set_ylabel('$f(x)$')
ax.set_title('Standard Cauchy vs. standard normal')
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

:::{.definition data-title="Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)"}

The cumulative distribution function is

$$
F(x) = \frac{1}{\pi} \arctan\!\left(\frac{x - x_0}{\gamma}\right)
  + \frac{1}{2}.
$$

:::

## Key Properties

:::{.theorem data-title="Non-Existence of Moments"}

For $X \sim \text{Cauchy}(x_0, \gamma)$, the expectation
$\mathbb{E}[X]$ does not exist, and consequently neither the variance nor
the moment generating function exists.

:::

:::{.proof}

For the standard Cauchy, $\mathbb{E}[|X|] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty
\frac{|x|}{\pi(1 + x^2)} \, dx$ diverges, since the integrand behaves
like $1/(\pi|x|)$ for large $|x|$. Hence $\mathbb{E}[X]$ is undefined and
no higher moments exist.

:::

The location $x_0$ is instead the **median** and **mode**, and $\gamma$
is the half-width at half-maximum.

## Characteristic Function

:::{.theorem data-title="Characteristic Function"}

Although the MGF does not exist, the characteristic function of
$X \sim \text{Cauchy}(x_0, \gamma)$ is well defined:

$$
\varphi_X(t) = \exp\!\left(i x_0 t - \gamma |t|\right).
$$

:::

A consequence is that the sample mean of $n$ i.i.d. standard Cauchy
variables is again standard Cauchy — averaging does **not** reduce
dispersion, in stark contrast to the Law of Large Numbers.

## Relationship to Other Distributions

- **[[normal-distribution]]:** If $Z_1, Z_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ are
  independent, then $Z_1/Z_2 \sim \text{Cauchy}(0, 1)$.
- **[[students-t-distribution]]:** The standard Cauchy is Student's $t$
  with one degree of freedom.
- **Stable distribution:** The Cauchy is one of the few stable
  distributions with a closed-form density, alongside the normal.

## Examples and Applications

:::{.example data-title="Ratio of normals"}

The ratio of two independent centred normal measurements — for example
the tangent of a uniformly random angle — follows a Cauchy distribution.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Resonance"}

In physics, the Cauchy (Lorentzian) distribution describes the shape of
spectral lines and the response of a driven resonant system.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Robustness testing"}

Because it lacks a mean, the Cauchy distribution is a standard stress
test for estimators and for the assumptions behind the Central Limit
Theorem.

:::
